title: Siadajcie, zupa na stole!
titleEn: Sit down, the soup’s on the table!
focus: family meals: offers and requests, imperatives, the “some” genitive, family vocatives

patterns.determinate: Determinate motion: now, in one direction

lines.speaker: Babcia
lines.pl: Siadajcie|siadajcie, siadajcie! Zupa już na stole|stole. Smacznego|smacznego!
lines.en: Sit down, sit down! The soup’s on the table. Enjoy your meal!

lines.speaker: Wujek Jurek
lines.pl: Mamo|mamo, rosół|rosol pachnie|pachnie jak zawsze. Tomek, podaj|podaj mi|mi sól|sol, proszę.
lines.en: Mum, the broth smells just like it always does. Tomek, pass me the salt, please.

lines.speaker: Babcia
lines.pl: Tomku|tomku, nałożyć|nalozyc ci|ci jeszcze zupy|zupy? Jesteś taki chudy|chudy!
lines.en: Tomek, shall I give you some more soup? You’re so thin!

lines.speaker: Tomek
lines.pl: Dziękuję, pani Zosiu|zosiu, ale zostawię|zostawie miejsce na drugie|drugie danie|danie.
lines.en: Thank you, Mrs. Zosia, but I’ll save room for the main course.

lines.speaker: Ciocia Basia
lines.pl: Na drugie są gołąbki|golabki i kotlety. Ania, przynieś|przynies ziemniaki z kuchni|kuchni, dobrze?
lines.en: For the main course there are cabbage rolls and pork cutlets. Ania, bring the potatoes from the kitchen, will you?

lines.speaker: Ania
lines.pl: Już niosę|niose. Ciociu|ciociu, a dla Kasi|kasi zrobiłaś|zrobilas coś bez mięsa|miesa?
lines.en: On my way. Auntie, did you make something without meat for Kasia?

lines.speaker: Ciocia Basia
lines.pl: Oczywiście! Pierogi ruskie|ruskie. Tylko zostawcie|zostawcie jej|jej trochę|troche, chłopcy|chlopcy!
lines.en: Of course! Pierogi ruskie. Just leave her some, boys!

lines.speaker: Babcia
lines.pl: A na deser|deser sernik|sernik. Kto nie zje|zje, ten nie dostanie|dostanie kompotu|kompotu!
lines.en: And for dessert, cheesecake. Anyone who doesn’t finish their plate gets no kompot!

lines.speaker: Wujek Jurek
lines.pl: Mamo, nikt|nikt tu nie umrze|umrze z głodu|glodu, obiecuję|obiecuje.
lines.en: Mum, nobody here is going to starve, I promise.

siadajcie.why: Invitations and encouragement normally use the imperfective imperative: siadajcie, jedzcie, częstujcie się. The perfective usiądźcie sounds more like an instruction.

stole.why: Na + locative: na stole, “on the table.” Zupa już na stole leaves out jest, which is common in quick spoken announcements.

smacznego.tags: adjective used as a wish · genitive singular
smacznego.why: Smacznego!, “enjoy your meal”, is a wish, so it’s genitive, short for życzę smacznego. Polish families say it at the start of every meal.

mamo.why: Jurek is talking to his own mother. Feminine nouns in -a take -o in the vocative: mama → mamo. Diminutives in -ia take -u instead: babcia → babciu, ciocia → ciociu.

rosol.why: Rosół, a clear chicken or beef broth with noodles, is the classic first course of a Polish Sunday dinner.

pachnie.why: Pachnieć is for pleasant smells. An unpleasant smell is śmierdzieć.

podaj.why: Podać is the verb for passing things at the table. The perfective imperative makes a concrete request; proszę at the end softens it.

mi.why: The person something is passed to is in the dative: podaj mi sól, podaj babci chleb.

sol.tags: noun · feminine · accusative singular (same as nominative)
sol.why: Sól is feminine but ends in a consonant, so its accusative looks like its nominative. Other forms open the ó to o: soli, solą.

tomku.why: Babcia calls Tomek by his first name, in the vocative, as older people often do with younger guests.

nalozyc.gloss: to serve (food), put on a plate
nalozyc.why: An infinitive question is an offer: nałożyć ci…?, “shall I give you…?” Nałożyć is for food on a plate; for drinks it’s nalać: nalać ci herbaty?

ci.why: The short dative of ty: nałożyć komuś, “to serve someone.”

zupy.why: Here the genitive means “some”: nałożyć zupy, “to serve some soup.” With the accusative, nałożyć zupę, you’d be serving the soup as a whole.

chudy.why: Masculine because Babcia is talking to Tomek. An adjective after być stays nominative.

you.m: Said to you: Jesteś taki chudy!
you.f: Said to you: Jesteś taka chuda!

zosiu.why: Diminutives in -ia take -u in the vocative. Pani with a diminutive first name is a warm but still polite way to address an older woman you know.

zostawie.why: Perfective, so the present form is future: “I’ll leave.” Zostawić miejsce na…, “to save room for…”

drugie.why: Drugie danie, “the second course”, is the main course; the first is the soup. Na drugie on its own means “for the main course.”

danie.tags: noun · neuter · accusative singular (same as nominative)
danie.why: Danie is formed from dać, “to give”: what is served. Na + accusative expresses purpose: na drugie danie, na deser.

golabki.why: Gołąbki are cabbage leaves wrapped around minced meat and rice, baked in tomato sauce. The name means “little pigeons.”

parts: root: carry; no ending in the imperative
przynies.why: The imperative of przynieść. Adding dobrze? at the end turns the instruction into a friendly request.

kuchni.why: Z + genitive, “from”: z kuchni. Nouns in -nia end in -ni in the genitive, dative and locative.

niose.tags: verb · imperfective · determinate · present · 1st person singular
niose.why: Nieść is the determinate “carry”, like iść for walking. Już niosę, “I’m bringing them right now.” Its indeterminate partner is nosić.

ciociu.why: Ciocia is itself a diminutive (of ciotka), and like other nouns in -ia it takes -u in the vocative. Children call any close family friend ciocia too.

kasi.why: Dla + genitive. Names in -ia have -i in the genitive: Kasia → Kasi, Ania → Ani.

zrobilas.tags: verb · perfective · past · 2nd person singular · feminine
zrobilas.why: Feminine because Ania is talking to her aunt. Within the family, aunts and uncles are addressed with ty.

miesa.why: Bez + genitive, “without”: bez mięsa, bez cukru.

parts: non-virile pl. -e (the i marks k softened)
ruskie.why: Pierogi ruskie are filled with potato, curd cheese and onion. Ruskie refers to historical Ruthenia (Ruś), not to Russia.

zostawcie.why: Plural imperative, aimed at the men at the table.

jej.why: Zostawić komuś coś, “to leave something for someone”: the person is in the dative.

troche.why: Like other words of quantity, trochę takes the genitive: trochę zupy, trochę czasu. Here the noun (pierogów) is understood.

chlopcy.why: In the plural, the vocative is always the same as the nominative. Said to grown men, chłopcy is affectionate and teasing.

deser.tags: noun · masculine inanimate · accusative singular (same as nominative)
deser.why: Na + accusative for purpose: na deser, “for dessert”; na obiad, “for lunch.”

sernik.why: Polish cheesecake is made with twaróg, a fresh curd cheese. The suffix -nik makes a noun from ser.

parts: present stem of jeść; 3rd sg. has no further ending
zje.why: Kto…, ten… means “whoever…, (they)…”. Perfective, because it’s about finishing the food.

parts: future stem dostan- (n softened before e)
dostanie.why: Dostać has the future stem dostan-: dostanę, dostaniesz, dostanie.

kompotu.why: Negation turns the object genitive: dostanie kompot → nie dostanie kompotu. Kompot, fruit simmered in water and served as a drink, is a fixture of Polish home dinners.

nikt.why: Polish uses double negation: nikt nie umrze, literally “nobody won’t die.”

umrze.why: Umrzeć is irregular: umrę, umrzesz, umrze; past umarł, umarła.

glodu.why: Z + genitive can give a cause: umrzeć z głodu, “to die of hunger”; płakać ze śmiechu, “to cry with laughter.”

obiecuje.why: Verbs in -ywać form their present with -uj-: obiecywać → obiecuję.

exercises.prompt: Ask someone to pass the bread: ___ mi chleb, proszę.
exercises.explain: The imperative of podać: Poda + j.

exercises.prompt: Offer some more tea (herbata): Nalać ci jeszcze ___?
exercises.explain: “Some” of a food or drink is genitive: herbaty.

exercises.prompt: Call your grandmother (babcia) to the table: ___, chodź do stołu!
exercises.explain: Nouns in -ia take -u in the vocative: babcia → babciu.

exercises.prompt: Tell your cousins to eat (imperative stem jedz-): ___!

exercises.explain: Negation turns the object genitive: kawy.
